title: The Transitus (3 October 1226)
hook: Francis dies lying on the bare ground singing Psalm 141

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peace prayer, honestly: not his words, but his shape. Your line was francis-shaped. What did you do that no one will sign his name to? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-six.

Evening, at the little church of Saint Mary of the Angels below Assisi. Francis is dying, and he knows it. His brothers are crowded around. He is blind or nearly, worn out, and the early lives say he carries wounds in his hands and side. And he asks for something strange. Take off my habit, he tells them, and lay me on the bare ground. No bed. No pillow. Just the earth he called sister and mother. Then, the old biographers say, he began to sing. Today, the night Francis died, and the name his brothers gave it.
screen: `EVENING, AT SAINT MARY OF THE ANGELS.` → `LAY ME ON THE BARE GROUND.` → `AND HE BEGAN TO SING.`

segments.voice: Franciscans call that night the Transitus, Latin for a passing over. Not an ending. A crossing. The word echoes the Gospel Francis asked to hear that evening, John chapter thirteen, which opens in the Douay-Rheims: "Jesus knowing that his hour was come, that he should pass out of this world to the Father." Francis wanted to die the way his Lord had passed: poor, stripped, among his friends. The early lives tell the scene in pieces. Francis blesses the brothers around him. He tells them, in Saint Bonaventure's telling, that he has done his part, and may Christ teach them theirs. And then he sings Psalm one hundred forty-one, as it's numbered in the Latin Bible the friars prayed. It begins: "I cried to the Lord with my voice." And near the end it asks: "Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name." A dying man asking to be let out of prison, and calling it praise. There's one more line that belongs to this night. Earlier, Francis had added a last verse to his Canticle of the Creatures, praising God for our Sister Bodily Death, whom no one living can escape. Celano tells that when death came near, Francis greeted it as family: welcome, my sister death. The man who called the sun brother called death sister too. Bonaventure adds a quiet detail: larks, birds of daylight, gathered over the roof at dusk and sang. Whether you hear that as a sign or a lovely story, the brothers remembered it.
screen: `TRANSITUS: A PASSING OVER.` · `JOHN 13: HIS HOUR WAS COME.` · `PSALM 141, SUNG ON THE BARE GROUND.` · `DEATH, GREETED AS A SISTER.` · then, large: `BRING MY SOUL OUT OF PRISON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lie down and pray a psalm. If you can, lie flat, on the floor or a bed, arms loose at your sides. If you can't, lean back and let your body be heavy. Feel the ground holding you up. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can say the line Francis sang: I cried to the Lord with my voice. Say it, and rest. Then the other one: bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name. If you don't pray, just notice how it feels to be held by the floor, with nothing to do. The bell holds the time.
The Transitus. Francis's passing over: dying on the bare ground, singing a psalm, greeting death as his sister. Today's word.
Your line: welcome, sister death. Today, when you lie down to sleep, take one slow breath and remember that Francis greeted even death as a sister. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Franciscans and some parishes keep a Transitus service on the eve of Saint Francis's feast, retelling his death with readings, Psalm 141 and his Canticle of the Creatures, often by candlelight.

original.note: Latin: a passing over, a crossing; the Franciscan name for the night of Francis's death.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Transitus is a fancy name for Francis's funeral.
what it means: his passing over, kept by Franciscans on the eve of his feast, with the psalm he sang on the bare ground.
what a scholar hears: Psalm 141 in the Latin numbering the friars prayed is Psalm 142 in Hebrew-based Bibles. the same psalm, two numbers.

notes: Claims rule: the title's date is not repeated in the voice. 'Psalm one hundred forty-one' is the index's own reference (Vulgate numbering); the trapdoor's renumbering note (Hebrew 142) should be confirmed.

Deathbed details paraphrased from Celano and Bonaventure: laid naked on the ground at the Portiuncula; blessing the brothers; 'I have done what is mine; may Christ teach you what is yours' (Bonaventure, LM 14.3); John 13 read aloud; Psalm 141 ('Voce mea ad Dominum clamavi') sung; larks over the roof at dusk (LM 14.6); 'Welcome, my sister death' (Celano, 2 Cel 217). Confirm each attribution.
'He is blind or nearly' and 'carrying wounds in his hands and side' (the stigmata) are stated from the early lives; confirm phrasing.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: John 13:1; Psalm 141:2 and 141:8.
howItsDone: confirm 'some parishes' keep a Transitus service; the date (evening of 3 October) is not stated.

Editor pass: the stigmata now attributed to the early lives rather than stated by the narrator; 'the word comes straight from the Gospel' (an etymology claim) softened to 'echoes'; the carry's garbled 'met even his last night as family' rewritten. John 13:1 and Psalm 141:2, 141:8 Douay-Rheims fragments checked.
